full_article:
Ganesh Parajuli

Kathmandu, October 28

A parliamentary special committee has stressed the need to make Nepal’s participation in the upcoming COP31 climate conference results-oriented, with a focus on climate justice, disaster-related loss and damage, and national interests.

The committee held a meeting on Wednesday to discuss the impacts of climate change on the Himalayas, climate justice, and disasters in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river basins. Discussions focused on Nepal’s participation in COP31, climate diplomacy and issues of national interest.

Committee Chair Ganesh Parajuli said Nepal’s participation in the conference should go beyond formal visits and focus on achieving concrete outcomes.

He stressed that representatives taking part in international negotiations and dialogues should have the necessary subject expertise, adequate preparation and the ability to effectively present Nepal’s interests.

The meeting also discussed the issues Nepal should raise at COP31 with the concerned minister, ministry secretaries and the chief of the environment division.

Participants emphasised that Nepal’s international negotiations should take into account the positions expressed by the prime minister at the United Nations and by the Speaker of the House of Representatives at the Inter-Parliamentary Union.

Parajuli said Nepal should use its pavilion and documentaries presented at the conference to highlight the damage caused by recent floods, landslides and other climate-related disasters.

At the same time, he stressed the importance of communicating a positive message to the international community that Nepal remains a safe and attractive destination for tourism, alongside highlighting the impacts of disasters.

The meeting also discussed a proposal to divide the committee’s 15 members into five groups, each comprising three members, to cover nine thematic areas. Further discussions will be held to assign responsibilities based on members’ interests and subject expertise.

The committee underscored the need to ensure that Nepal’s participation in COP31 delivers tangible outcomes on climate justice, loss and damage caused by disasters, and other issues of national interest.

title: Nepal proposes regional space cooperation for monitoring climate risks - The Rising Nepal
description: Nepal proposes regional space cooperation for monitoring climate risks  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Oct 28: Nepal has put forth three proposals on disaster preparedness in the ongoing 'Fifth Ministerial Conference on Space Applications for Sustainable Development in Asia and the Pacific' underway in Thailand.

Minister for Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation, Biraj Bhakta Shrestha, floated the proposal of Asia Pacific level cooperation for space monitoring of climate hazards during the conference organized by the UN Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP) in Bangkok on Wednesday. The event is being held from October 28 to 29.

In his address on the theme of 'Harnessing space applications for a resilient and inclusive future through enhanced regional cooperation' in the conference, Minister Shrestha said time has come for forging a regional cooperation with space technology in order to cope with increasing disasters posed by climate change.

"Nepal wishes to highlight three priorities for our collective consideration. First, establish high-mountain hazards as a sustained priority of regional space cooperation. We encourage systematic satellite monitoring of unstable slopes and glacial lakes as an integral part of regional monitoring and early warning arrangements. Second, translate data into practical guidance for timely action. Alongside access to satellite imagery, countries need ready-to-use information, shared analytical tools and trained professionals who can support informed decisions when every minute matters. Third, ensure equitable and affordable access to space-based information and services. All countries should be able to benefit from these capabilities, regardless of whether they operate their own satellites, particularly when human lives are at risk," the Minister explained in the address.

Minister Shrestha informed the global community that Nepal’s recent experience shows urgent need to strengthen our ability to understand and respond to complex disasters. "We can turn space-based information into practical decisions, and regional cooperation into services that people can use," he said, adding that the Asia Pacific has growing satellite capabilities, more open data and powerful digital tools. But, many institutions are in dire need of skills, resources and systems to use them in their daily work.

Closing this gap is a priority for Nepal, Minister Shrestha reminded. He shared that on the morning of August 26, nearly 680,000 text warnings had reached mobile phones along the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river corridor. In October, around 200,000 more helped communities downstream move to safety.

The Minister brought to light the study that ICIMOD and UNDP had identified 47 potentially dangerous glacial lakes across three Himalayan river basins shared by Nepal, China and India. Twenty-one of them are in Nepal. "With the Green Climate Fund and UNDP, Nepal has begun work to lower and monitor four of the most dangerous: Thulagi, Lower Barun, Lumding and Hongu," he informed.

Shrestha further argued because it is not possible to build concrete on each mountain, many slopes and lakes are not reachable. So, the eyes must be in space. "We need continuous satellite observation of glaciers, lakes and slopes, checked against measurements on the ground. We need artificial intelligence to sift what the satellites see, and digital simulations that show how a hazard would travel downstream. Above all, that knowledge must reach decision-makers and families in time," Shrestha addressed.

The Minister viewed a satellite can detect a danger in the mountains. "Only a warning that reaches a family downstream can save a life. The river systems of the Hindu Kush Himalaya support the lives and livelihoods of nearly two billion people. Their protection is a shared regional responsibility."

He underscored need of ensuring practical impact of collective efforts as the Asia-Pacific Plan of Action advances towards 2030.

Minister Shrestha will also address another event at Asian Institute of Technology on Thursday. He is scheduled to return home coming Saturday. (RSS)

Morrison and his partner Hilaree Nelson aspired to summit Mount Everest’s north side, something only five people had ever done. None had ever skied down it. Given the long stream of mountaineers that queue up on the south face, you could call it the most drastic feat ever of avoiding a lift line.

“Everest: The Other Side,” by “Free Solo” filmmakers Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin, is the big-screen chronicle of Morrison and Nelson’s mission. Theirs is a quixotic aspiration: climb the world’s highest peak and then coast down.

But “Everest: The Other Side” is as much a document of tragedy and grief as it is one of extreme sport. On a similar expedition in 2022 while biding their time for Everest, Morrison and Nelson — partners in love and adventure — reached the top of a Nepalese mountain. But after just a few turns on her skis, a sheet of snow dislodged underneath Nelson. She died in the avalanche.

Nelson’s death reverberated through the mountaineering world and it reshaped the film Vasarhelyi and Chin were making. In “Free Solo,” which documents Alex Honnold ascending El Capitan in Yosemite without ropes or a harness, the filmmakers had to contemplate the possibility that Honnold might fall to his death.

In “Everest,” that awful possibility comes to pass. Nelson’s fatal fall, as well as Morrison’s recovery of her body two days later, is captured with agonizing IMAX clarity. If “Free Solo” was about an unmitigated triumph, “Everest” wrestles with a darker side of such perilous exploits.

“This movie, the worst happened,” Vasarhelyi says in a brief moment on screen.

Risk tolerance is a common topic for Vasarhelyi and Chin, filmmakers who have intrepidly fused nature documentaries with adventure drama. Chin is himself a decorated climber; he summited and skied down the south face of Everest in 2006.

But in “Everest,” questioning whether it’s worth it is front and center. The movie lingers on the moments when Morrison and his team leave their homes, parting with children for two-month stints during which they’ll risk their lives on desolate peaks on the other side of the world. When Nelson dies, she leaves behind two boys. As the years tick on in the documentary, we watch them grow up without their mother.

Yet within months of her death, Morrison, from his lakeside Tahoe home, resolves to push ahead with the Everest climb. Tragedy isn’t new to him. Years earlier, he lost his wife, Katie, and two children, Wyatt and Hannah, in a plane crash. After first finding a walk down the driveway an insurmountable hike, Morrison resolves to live for them.

So his aim to reach the top of Everest and ski down may be a daredevil feat, but it’s also a grieving, heavy-hearted quest. He describes his yearning to ride down “the raddest ski line in the world.” But what’s compelling him is also something that can’t be easily articulated.

“Everest: The Other Side” is, to a certain extent, alive to these quandaries. The filmmakers even share in them. Chin accompanies Morrison on both an aborted ascent and the successful attempt in 2025.

Deciding to continue with the project is its own debate for Chin and Vasarhelyi. They have two children of their own. Their proximity to extreme expeditions has already brought tragedy close to home. “How many people who have eaten at our dinner table have died?” Vasarhelyi asks him. The couple divorced in 2025, though their separation goes unmentioned in the film.

While these debates are often present in the documentary, “Everest: The Other Side” grows increasingly shy of them. The higher Morrison climbs, the less inquisitive the movie gets. On the first attempted ascent, some of the Sherpas grow wary of the risks involved. Their sensible hesitations don’t put Morrison, handsomely outfitted by his North Face sponsor, in the best light.

By the time Morrison realizes his dream, it feels as though many have, off camera, moved on with their lives. The families back home fall out of the movie. “Everest: The Other Side” becomes a mournful and increasingly solitary march.

Maybe that’s appropriate. Morrison’s extreme compulsion inevitably pulls him away from us, leaving behind a more disquieting film. Even he can’t help but notice while hiking up that the snow conditions he’ll be skiing down are rock hard and terrible. The descent, lasting four hours, is a feat of skill, perseverance and bravery. Even on a bad day, he’d have to grant, the skiing would have been better back home.

“Everest: The Other Side,” a Walt Disney Co. release in theaters Friday, is rated PG-13 by the Motion Picture Association for thematic material and brief strong language. Running time: 115 minutes. Two and a half stars out of four.
